sentences.text: Now the vessels that aren’t moving.
At anchor, the interval is shorter: not more than one minute.
A vessel at anchor, under one hundred meters, rings her bell rapidly for about five seconds.
A vessel of one hundred meters or more rings the bell in the fore part, and then immediately sounds the gong in the after part, about five seconds each.
Bell forward, gong aft, so you can hear how long she is.
A vessel at anchor may also sound three blasts, one short, one prolonged, one short, to warn an approaching vessel of her position.
But a vessel engaged in fishing at anchor, or a restricted vessel working at anchor, doesn’t ring the bell.
She sounds one prolonged and two short instead, the same hampered signal she’d use underway, every two minutes.
And a vessel aground gives the bell signal with something extra: three separate, distinct strokes on the bell before the rapid ringing, and three more after.
So in fog, a rapid bell means a vessel at anchor.
And three strokes, a rapid bell, and three strokes means she’s aground, so don’t follow her in.
